title: Job 16:1–17
context: Job answers Eliphaz’s second speech (Job 15), and the whole of chapters 16–17 is Job’s reply. He begins by calling his friends miserable comforters whose words bring no relief, recalling that they first came to comfort him (Job 2:11) and that he has already called them physicians of no value (Job 13:4); his complaint of vain words may answer Eliphaz’s own charge of vain knowledge (Job 15:2–3). Job says he could speak as they do, but he would strengthen them instead. He then turns to God with a raw lament, speaking to him and about him: God has worn him out, shriveled him, torn him in wrath, handed him to the wicked, seized him by the neck, set him up as a target, and run at him like a giant. Some interpreters take the adversary of verse 9 to be God, and others human enemies; the surrounding lines speak of God directly. Job ends by insisting that there is no violence in his hands and that his prayer is pure. These are Job’s words in the middle of the dialogue, not the book’s settled verdict; the narrator has already called Job blameless (Job 1:1), and the LORD’s speeches and 42:7 come later. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the lament as the honest cry of a suffering righteous man, one the book does not condemn as the friends do.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Job now answers Eliphaz’s second speech. His reply continues the dialogue in which the friends press their explanation of his suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job taking his turn in the debate. Readers in both traditions commonly read the speech as Job’s own words, not the book’s settled verdict on his case.

verses.text: “I have heard many such things. You are all miserable comforters!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job calling his friends miserable comforters. Those who came to comfort him (Job 2:11) have added to his pain instead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s complaint as a sober warning about counsel that wounds rather than heals. Readers in both traditions commonly take the friends as sincere but mistaken, without demonizing them.

verses.text: Shall vain words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job asking whether vain words will ever end, perhaps answering Eliphaz’s charge of vain knowledge (Job 15:2). The debate has grown sharp.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see frustration with speech that does not fit the sufferer’s situation. Both traditions commonly hear a lesson about speaking carefully to those in pain.

verses.text: I also could speak as you do. If your soul were in my soul’s place, I could join words together against you, and shake my head at you,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying he could speak as they do and shake his head at them if their places were reversed. Easy judgment is always available.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job exposing how simple it is to lecture a sufferer from a safe distance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as an appeal for empathy.

verses.text: but I would strengthen you with my mouth. The solace of my lips would relieve you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying he would instead strengthen them with his mouth and relieve them with his words. Comfort should build up the hurting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a picture of the comfort that friends owe one another (compare Romans 12:15; Galatians 6:2). Both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a model of pastoral care.

verses.text: “Though I speak, my grief is not subsided. Though I forbear, what am I eased?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying that neither speaking nor keeping silent eases his grief. His pain does not lift either way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an honest description of suffering that words cannot fix. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with compassion rather than correction.

verses.text: But now, God, you have surely worn me out. You have made all my company desolate.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job speaking directly to God and saying he has worn him out and made his company desolate. Job does not hide his complaint from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job bringing his grief straight to God rather than away from him. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the honest lament of a righteous sufferer.

verses.text: You have shriveled me up. This is a witness against me. My leanness rises up against me. It testifies to my face.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying his shriveled body has become a witness against him. His condition seems to testify that he is guilty, as the friends assume.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job feeling his suffering used as evidence against his integrity. Readers in both traditions commonly note that the book has already called Job blameless (Job 1:1).

verses.text: He has torn me in his wrath and persecuted me. He has gnashed on me with his teeth. My adversary sharpens his eyes on me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job describing being torn in wrath, gnashed at, and watched by an adversary. They generally let the accusation stand as Job’s honest cry, not the book’s doctrine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same raw language and do not soften it. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as the cry of a suffering righteous man whom the book does not condemn as the friends do.

verses.text: They have gaped on me with their mouth. They have struck me on the cheek reproachfully. They gather themselves together against me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job describing people gaping at him, striking his cheek, and gathering against him. Human scorn adds to his anguish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see language that echoes the psalms of the afflicted (compare Psalm 22:13). Both traditions commonly hear the sufferer’s isolation, and some later note echoes in Christ’s sufferings.

verses.text: God delivers me to the ungodly, and casts me into the hands of the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying God delivers him to the ungodly. They generally take this as Job’s perception from inside his pain, held alongside the book’s wider account of his trial.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job attributing his troubles to God without flinching. Readers in both traditions commonly let the statement stand as Job’s lament rather than turning it into a settled doctrinal claim.

verses.text: I was at ease, and he broke me apart. Yes, he has taken me by the neck, and dashed me to pieces. He has also set me up for his target.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying he was at ease until God broke him apart and set him up as a target. The image is violent and honest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image found also in Lamentations 3:12. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the language of lament, spoken by one who feels attacked by God.

verses.text: His archers surround me. He splits my kidneys apart, and does not spare. He pours out my bile on the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job describing archers surrounding him and God not sparing him. Job feels wounded to the core of his being.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see vivid lament language that does not hold back. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as Job’s experience of overwhelming suffering, not a calm theological statement.

verses.text: He breaks me with breach on breach. He runs at me like a giant.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying God breaks him with breach on breach and runs at him like a giant. Blow follows blow without relief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of a warrior assaulting a wall. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the honest cry of a man who feels besieged by God.

verses.text: I have sewed sackcloth on my skin, and have thrust my horn in the dust.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job sewing sackcloth on his skin and putting his horn in the dust. His strength and dignity are laid low.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outward signs of mourning and humiliation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of deep grief.

verses.text: My face is red with weeping. Deep darkness is on my eyelids,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job’s face red with weeping and deep darkness on his eyelids. Grief has marked his body as well as his heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the physical toll of long sorrow (compare Psalm 6:6). Both traditions commonly read the verse with compassion for the sufferer’s exhaustion.

verses.text: although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job insisting there is no violence in his hands and his prayer is pure. He maintains his integrity against the friends’ charges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s claim as consistent with the narrator’s verdict (Job 1:1), while still awaiting God’s answer. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a protest of innocence, not a claim of sinlessness.
